expected_evidence: Geological: Younger Dryas Boundary (YDB) sedimentary markers across North American sites — platinum/iridium anomalies, magnetic microspherules, nanodiamonds (lonsdaleite/cubic), glassy/melted spherules, and a 'black mat' organic-rich layer dated to ~10,950 BCE
Geological: continental-scale soot/charcoal spikes in lake and bog cores indicating widespread biomass burning coincident with the boundary layer
Material/archaeological: a documented drop or discontinuity in Clovis-age site density, artifact deposition rates, or occupation intensity immediately after the proposed impact date
Genetic: a detectable bottleneck or founder-effect signature in Paleoamerican mitochondrial/Y-chromosome or autosomal lineages dating to this interval, implying a demographic crash
Material/geological: megafaunal extinction pulse (mammoth, mastodon, etc.) stratigraphically aligned with the YDB layer, used as a proxy for ecosystem/human population stress
Astronomical: independent confirmation of an impact source — a crater, airburst structure, or cosmic-ray-exposure-dated fragments; notably absent/unconfirmed in current literature despite search

Oral_tradition: Indigenous North American narratives describing catastrophic fire, darkness, or sky-events potentially encoding memory of the event (low reliability given ~13,000-year transmission depth)
Iconographic: rock art or petroglyph motifs some researchers interpret as depicting a cometary/impact event (highly speculative, contested dating)
Textual: none expected — no writing systems existed in North America at this time
response.rationale: The interval (-10950) aligns with the onset of the Younger Dryas, so I applied the 'younger-dryas' row rather than treating the period as truly unspecified (flagged as inference, not given fact). The hypothesis bundles two claims: (1) a cosmic-impact/ejecta-fallout event occurred, and (2) it is 'corroborated' as affecting population-demography in North America. Evidence for claim (1) is primarily geological/astronomical, which have the highest detectability in this period (0.65 and 0.7 respectively) — and indeed this is realistic: YDB proponents (Firestone et al. 2007 and successors) have reported platinum, nanodiamond, and spherule layers at numerous North American sites, so this class of evidence is exactly what the real literature debate centers on (its existence is contested on interpretation/reproducibility grounds, not on total absence — consistent with moderate-high detectability). However, no confirmed crater or independently dated impactor has been found, which is expected under this same high-detectability astronomical category, since a real absence there is more informative (lower likelihood the event happened as a discrete impactor rather than an airburst leaving no crater). Evidence for claim (2), demographic impact specifically, relies on genetic (0.3) and material/archaeological (0.35) proxies, both markedly lower detectability for the Upper Paleolithic/Younger Dryas transition: ancient DNA coverage for Paleoamericans in this window is sparse, and site-density declines are confounded by taphonomic loss, survey bias, and alternative causal explanations (climate, overhunting). Oral tradition (0.1) and iconographic (0.1) evidence are essentially unfalsifiable at this time depth and should not be weighted heavily even if absent. Textual evidence is correctly expected to be absent (0.0) since no writing existed — this null category should not count against the hypothesis at all. Given this mix, the overall detectability is moderate: the impact-mechanism evidence is plausible to detect and partially has been (with ongoing scientific controversy over signal reliability), but the specific demographic-corroboration claim is much harder to substantiate given low genetic/archaeological detectability for this period. This pattern is consistent with the real-world state of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis: geological signals are reported but contested, while a clean demographic causal link to North American population decline remains empirically thin — an absence better explained by low genetic/demographic-proxy detectability than by outright falsity of a hypothetical impact event.
